meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Part Went for Liquor, Part for Women; The Rest I Spent Foolishly'?
meta.ogDescription: A 1936 Reader’s Digest joke about an anonymous sailor. George Raft and Tug McGraw each told a version of their own; none of them originated it, and George Best inherited a different line marked only “Attr.”

answer.label: Not George Best — a 1936 magazine gag
answer.authorDates: Credited submitter, The Reader’s Digest, August 1936 · which Channing Pollock is uncertain
answer.sourceLine: The exact wording is a stock joke about an anonymous sailor, printed in The Reader’s Digest in August 1936 and credited to a contributor named Channing Pollock — nearly a decade before George Best was born. Best is linked to a different variant (“booze, birds and fast cars… the rest I just squandered”), and even that reaches print marked simply “Attr.” with no citation.

source.excerpt: Do you remember the sailor who, asked what he’d done with his wages, answered, “Part went for liquor, part for women, and the rest I spent foolishly.”? — Channing Pollock
trail: August 1936 — the earliest printing anyone has found. Quote Investigator ↗ locates the joke in The Reader’s Digest, Vol. 29, No. 172, p. 46, in a column of illustrative anecdotes, submitted by a contributor named Channing Pollock and told about an anonymous sailor.

The same month, on the other side of the country. The researcher Bill Mullins found a second 1936 instance in Pacific Coast Magic News, where a magician at a post-convention party in Oakland gives the same answer about liquor, women and the rest spent foolishly — evidence, as QI notes ↗, that the gag was already circulating freely.

Decades of new owners. George Raft in 1966, Tug McGraw in 1975, and by 1993 the footballer Frank Worthington, whose version — crediting the punchline to Stan Bowles — was printed in The Independent on 10 September 1995 ↗.

2000 onwards — Best inherits it. A Times reference book files a “booze, birds and fast cars” variant under his name marked “Attr.”, and the press repeats it, including BBC News on 14 June 2005 ↗, which runs it as a pull-quote with no source at all.
source.excerptNote: Quoted as transcribed by Quote Investigator, which records the Reader’s Digest citation as verified on paper. Note the opening words: even here the joke is being recalled, not coined.

source.rightsNote: No public-domain claim is available here under any reading. The wording’s true origin is an unattributed circulating joke with no identifiable author, and the earliest printing anyone has documented — The Reader’s Digest, August 1936 — falls well after the 1931 United States cut-off in any case. The George Best variant reaches print later still, through in-copyright reference and news publishing of 2000 and after, so we assert no rights status for either wording.

author.name: Channing Pollock
author.heading: The man in the 1936 credit line
author.metaLine: Credited in The Reader’s Digest, August 1936 · identity uncertain
author.bio: Channing Pollock is the name printed beside the earliest known appearance of this joke — a reader submission to The Reader’s Digest in August 1936. Quote Investigator is careful here, and so are we: a Channing Pollock (1880–1946) was an American playwright and drama critic; a second Channing Pollock, the movie-star magician, was only ten in 1936 and is ruled out on age. QI still declines to confirm the playwright is the submitter — “it is not certain that the joke submitter Channing Pollock is the same individual.” Pollock’s own phrasing suggests he was not the author either: he opens with “Do you remember the sailor who…”, which is how you retell a joke, not how you coin one.

copyAttribution: Not George Best. "Part went for liquor, part for women, and the rest I spent foolishly" is a stock gag printed in The Reader's Digest in August 1936 (vol. 29, no. 172, p. 46), credited to a contributor named Channing Pollock and told about an anonymous sailor — nearly a decade before Best was born in May 1946. The same joke has changed hands for decades — George Raft (1966) and Tug McGraw (1975) each told a version of their own, and it reached football via Stan Bowles — but none of them originated it. Best's own variant, "I spent a lot of money on booze, birds and fast cars. The rest I just squandered," appears in The Times Book of Quotations (2000) marked only "Attr.", with no source. Traced by Quote Investigator, "Part Went for Liquor, Part for Women; The Rest I Spent Foolishly" (19 May 2010).

misattribution.heading: Everyone who has been handed this joke
misattribution.intro: This is not one misattribution but a queue of them. The line is a floating gag, and Quote Investigator documents it changing owners for the better part of a century — each new host a famous man who had spectacularly run through his money.

items.why: Best is credited with a different variant: “I spent a lot of money on booze, birds and fast cars. The rest I just squandered.” The earliest instance Quote Investigator cites for it is The Times Book of Quotations (2000), p. 249 — which prints it under the flat label “Attr.”, gives no source, and files the Belfast-born Best as an “English footballer.” The BBC repeated it in 2002 and again in a news article of 14 June 2005 ↗, still with no source. Nothing found anywhere puts the “part went for liquor” wording in his mouth.

The Hollywood star is quoted with “Part of the loot went for gambling, part for horses and part for women. The rest I spent foolishly” in a Parade profile of 23 October 1966 and again in his 1980 obituary. Quote Investigator ↗ accepts that Raft used it — but places him thirty years after the joke was already in print.

The baseball pitcher’s line on his new salary — ninety per cent on good times, women and Irish whiskey, the other ten per cent he would probably waste — ran in Sports Illustrated’s “They Said It” column on 21 April 1975, and Quote Investigator ↗ treats it as genuine.

The Independent, 10 September 1995 ↗, prints a 1993 remark by Frank Worthington about squandering fortunes on birds, booze and gambling, with the punchline credited to “my old pal Stan Bowles” — so even inside football the joke was being passed along, not invented.

items.who: A sailor, a hobo, a marine, a cat skinner
items.why: Quote Investigator’s full-text searching turns up the same structure with an unnamed spender throughout, including a magician at a post-convention party in Oakland in Pacific Coast Magic News in the very same month as the Reader’s Digest printing, August 1936.

misattribution.truthLine: The exact wording belongs to no celebrity at all: it is a joke about an anonymous sailor, printed in The Reader’s Digest in August 1936 and credited to Channing Pollock — who opens “Do you remember the sailor who…”, which reads as a retelling rather than a coining. Quote Investigator ↗, which traced that printing, puts it no more firmly than “created or popularized by Channing Pollock by 1936.”

context.heading: A joke that keeps changing hosts
lead: Some quotations are misattributed once. This one is a floating gag — a joke with no fixed owner that reattaches itself to whichever famous spendthrift is currently in the papers. Quote Investigator found the money spent on wine, whiskey, booze, liquor, women, horses, gambling, “the finest duds” and three mustache curlers, and the spender identified as a sailor, a hobo, a marine, a cat skinner, the film star George Raft, the pitcher Tug McGraw and the footballers Stan Bowles and George Best.

Best is simply the most recent and most quotable host. He had the biography the joke needs — a Manchester United career he first walked out on at twenty-six and a very public life of drinking — and once a line fits a man that well, nobody checks it. The 2000 reference book that fixed it to his name did not even get his nationality right, listing the Belfast-born Best as an “English footballer.”
context.detailsSummary: Why the wording matters more than the sentiment
detailsBody: It is worth separating two claims that usually get muddled. The sentiment — I blew a fortune and cannot account for the last of it — is genuinely part of how Best talked about himself, and no one disputes that. The wording in this quotation is a different matter: it belongs to a 1936 gag Best never used.

Best’s own version is not the one people search for either. What he is credited with is “I spent a lot of money on booze, birds and fast cars. The rest I just squandered” — and the earliest instance Quote Investigator cites for it is a reference book of 2000, printed without a date, a venue or an interviewer. Wikiquote carries the line too, but its only citation is a BBC news article of 2005 that also gives no source. That is a chain of repetitions, not evidence.
context.pull: Even in 1936 it arrives second-hand: “Do you remember the sailor who…”

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator's earliest located instance is Reader's Digest, August 1936, p. 46, Vol. 29 No. 172, submitted by Channing Pollock, about a sailor: "Part went for liquor, part for women, and the rest I spent foolishly." QI concludes the joke was "created or popularized by Channing Pollock by 1936", notes a same-month sighting in Pacific Coast Magic News found by Bill Mullins, documents George Raft (Parade, 23 Oct 1966; 1980 obituary), Tug McGraw (Sports Illustrated, 21 Apr 1975), Frank Worthington/Stan Bowles (The Independent, 1995), and reproduces The Times Book of Quotations (2000), p. 249 crediting George Best with "I spent a lot of money on booze, birds and fast cars. The rest I just squandered. Attr." and labelling him an "English footballer". QI also states it is not certain which Channing Pollock submitted the joke.

Wikiquote's George Best page gives his dates as 22 May 1946 – 25 November 2005, describes him as Northern Irish, lists "I spent a lot of money on booze, birds and fast cars. The rest I just squandered." under the plain "Quotes" heading sourced only to the BBC News article "Best: Decline of the golden boy" (14 June 2005), and has no Misattributed or Disputed section (headings are Quotes, About George Best, External links).

BBC News, "Best: Decline of the golden boy", last updated Tuesday 14 June 2005, carries the pull-quote "I spent a lot of money on booze, birds and fast cars - the rest I just squandered" attributed to George Best, with no source, date or occasion given for the remark.

The Independent, "Demons on the loose" by Andrew Baker, Sunday 10 September 1995, prints: "I've squandered fortunes in my life on birds, booze and gambling. But, as my old pal Stan Bowles liked to say, it's better than wasting it." — Frank Worthington, 1993.

Google Books' record for The Reader's Digest, Volume 29 (DeWitt Wallace and Lila Acheson Wallace, Reader's Digest Association, 1936) reports "1 page matching 'spent foolishly' in this book", corroborating at catalog level that the phrase appears in that 1936 volume. The volume is snippet view only; no page image is viewable.

Wikipedia's article on Channing Pollock (writer) opens: "Channing Pollock (March 4, 1880 – August 17, 1946) was an American playwright, critic and screenwriter". Used only to describe the candidate Quote Investigator names, not to identify the 1936 joke submitter, whom QI expressly declines to identify.

Wikipedia's George Best article gives his birth as 22 May 1946 in Belfast and death as 25 November 2005 in London, describes him as a Northern Irish winger who played mainly for Manchester United, and attributes to him the quote "I spent a lot of money on booze, birds and fast cars. The rest I just squandered."
